text: You won't believe it!
Jaisalmer's Golden Fort is built from a seafloor, 160 million years old.
So how did a sea die and become the Thar?
Shark swam here. Sea reptiles hunted right where tourists now take selfies.
Today, Jaisalmer gets less than 200 millimeters of rain in a whole year.
Mumbai has seen more than that fall in a single day.
To find out, we're going to stand right here on the fort's hill
and rewind the clock 180 million years.
On the way, we'll meet a dinosaur nobody knew about until 2023, a lake near Bikaner
that vanished, a river that simply walked away, and a Sahara full of hippos.
And at the end, something strange that is happening to the Thar right now.
Let's rewind!
180 million years ago.
No sand, no camels, and India isn't even here.
It's stuck to Africa, Antarctica, and Australia in one giant southern landmass.
And right where the fort will one day stand, there's a forest.
Its trees turn to stone, and you can still see them today at Akal, near Jaisalmer.
One fallen trunk is over 13 meters long.
Longer than a bus, 180 million years of standing.
Finally, I get to lie down.
Ten million years later, the sea rolls in.
A warm, shallow ocean called the Tethys spreads over western Rajasthan.
The fort's hill is now underwater.
Its floor fills up with shells and lime mud.
Over millions of years, that mud hardens into golden yellow stone.
The same stone Jaisalmer's fort is built from.
Crack it open and you find shark teeth, ammonites, sea crocodiles, even a plesiosaur, a long-necked
reptile that swam these waters.
And on the shore, about 167 million years ago, walked Thorosaurus, a long-necked plant
eater, found near Jaisalmer and named in 2023.
It's the oldest known dinosaur of its family anywhere on Earth, oldest of my kind on the
whole planet, and you only noticed me in 2023?
Now fast forward to about 90 million years ago.
India breaks free and drifts north across the ocean, carrying Rajasthan along for the
ride. Around 50 million years ago, it slams into Asia. The crash pushes up the
Himalayas, and they're still rising today. But the sea doesn't leave quietly.
About 47 million years ago, whales were swimming near Jaisalmer. The
Geological Survey of India has dug up their fossils. Over the next few million
years, the land rises and the water drains away. The old seabed is now dry
land. But hold on, if the sea is gone, where does all this sand come from? Not from Rajasthan.
Much of it started in the mountains. Rivers like the Indus grind the rock down, carry it south,
and dump it on their floodplains in Delta. Then the summer monsoon blows in from the southwest
and picks it up. Grain by grain, it blows that sand inland. The very winds that should bring
rain are building a desert.
And the Thar is old.
Its dunes were already on the move more than 150,000 years ago.
So if you've heard it's only 4,000 years old or that humans made it, that's not what
the evidence says.
Back to today!
So why don't those monsoon winds drop their rain here?
Picture a pressure cooker lid.
Moist monsoon air comes in low, but high above it, hot, dry air from Arabia sits on top like
a lid.
The wet air can't climb high enough to build rain clouds, and the coast of Kuchen Sind
has no tall mountains to force the air up.
On the other side, the Western Ghats do exactly that, and soak Mumbai.
You'll often hear the Aravallis get the blame for running the wrong way.
That's only part of the story.
So that's how a sea became the Thar.
The sea drained away, rivers brought the sand, the monsoon wind built the dunes, and a lid
of dry air keeps the rain away.
But the Thar hasn't always been this dry.
When the monsoon grows stronger, the desert pulls back.
About 8,000 years ago, a big river, the Sutlej, changed course and abandoned its
old valley.
That dry riverbed, the Gagarhakara, still crosses northern Rajasthan.
Many people link it to the lost Saraswati.
Later, Harappan towns like Kalibangan grew along that old channel, fed by monsoon rain.
Near Bikaner, at Lunkaransar, there was a real lake.
For a couple of thousand years it held water.
Then, more than 5,000 years ago, it dried out.
And about 4,100 years ago, a drought hit northwest India.
Not one bad year. Around 200 years. Your whole life and your grandchildren's.
Around the same time, Harappan cities started emptying out. Many scientists think the two are linked.
Now here's the thing. Between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, while that lake near Beacon Air still held water, far to the west, the Sahara was green.
Not a little greener. Grassland, trees, rivers, hippos, crocodiles, giraffes, and
elephants lived where there's only sand today. Sahara, lakefront property. What
could possibly go wrong? People painted them on rock walls. In one cave in Egypt
the paintings even seem to show people swimming. And in the middle sat Lake
Megachad, about 360,000 square kilometers. Bigger than the whole of
Rajasthan, likely the largest freshwater lake on Earth at the time.
Today, Lake Chad is about one-tenth of one percent of that size.
So what flipped the switch?
Earth wobbles like a spinning top.
Every 20,000 years or so, that wobble changes how much summer sun hits North Africa.
More sun, stronger monsoon, green Sahara.
Less sun, the rain retreats, and it dries out.
It has flipped like this again and again for hundreds of thousands of years.
And just like the Thar, the Sahara used to be sea.
In Egypt's Valley of the Whales lie 40 million-year-old whale skeletons with tiny back legs.
Today, the Sahara is huge, around 9 million square kilometers.
You could fit almost three indias inside it, or about 40 Thars.
And only about a quarter of it is sand dunes.
Most of it is bare rock and gravel.
Here's the wildest part.
The dried-up bed of Lake Megachad, a place called Bodilei, is now the biggest dust source on Earth.
Every year, winds carry about 28 million tons of Saharan dust across the Atlantic into the Amazon.
With it comes about 22,000 tons of phosphorus, fertilizer for the rainforest.
Free fertilizer, Amazon. No need to thank me.
Back to the Thar, today.
On 19 May 2016, Falodi hit 51 degrees Celsius, the highest temperature ever recorded in India.
And yet the Thar is one of the most crowded deserts on earth.
Villages, towns, whole cities like Jodhpur and Bikaner, because people brought water.
The Indira Gandhi Canal carries water from Punjab 649 kilometers into the desert.
That's more than twice the distance from Delhi to Jaipur. And now the twist.
West. Satellites show the Thar got about 38% greener between 2001 and 2023. Rainfall over
it went up too, by about 64%. Meanwhile, the Sahara has grown by about 10% since 1920.
Two deserts. Both once seas. Both once green. Now heading in opposite directions. And Earth's
wobble never stops. Some day, the Sahara will turn green again.
So, next time you see Jaisalmer's golden walls, remember, you're looking at a seafloor
more than 160 million years old.
